title: Sonnet on Chillon: date and occasion
short: Written in late June 1816 after Byron and Shelley visited the Castle of Chillon on Lake Geneva; published with The Prisoner of Chillon on 5 December 1816.
body: On their boat tour round Lake Geneva, Byron and Shelley visited Chillon, probably on 26 June 1816, and were held by bad weather at Ouchy near Lausanne, where Byron wrote The Prisoner of Chillon (E. H. Coleridge). The sonnet was prefixed to the poem. Byron confessed in an 'Advertisement' that when he wrote the tale he knew too little of Bonivard's history to celebrate his courage and virtues, and he appended a French account of his life. The sonnet therefore makes Bonivard a public martyr of liberty, while the narrative poem dwells on the psychological ruin of an imprisoned man. The first draft opened 'Belovéd Goddess of the chainless mind!'

sources.cite: E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet
Jerome J. McGann, ed., Lord Byron: The Complete Poetical Works, vol. 4 (Oxford, 1986), commentary on the Sonnet on Chillon

title: the chainless Mind
short: The mind cannot be chained: liberty lives in the spirit even when the body is fettered.
body: The idea is a Stoic and Christian commonplace, given its best-known English form in Richard Lovelace's 'To Althea, from Prison' (published 1649): 'Stone walls do not a prison make, / Nor iron bars a cage.' Byron's opening apostrophe addresses Liberty as an 'Eternal Spirit', giving the political ideal a quasi-divine status. The sonnet's argument is that imprisonment makes freedom shine brighter, a paradox the narrative poem it introduces largely contradicts.

sources.cite: Richard Lovelace, 'To Althea, from Prison' (1649)
E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet

title: 'Brightest in dungeons'
short: Liberty shines most brightly in the darkness of prison, as a light in a vault.
body: The paradox of light in darkness runs through the octave, set against 'the damp vault's dayless gloom' (l. 6). The inversion ('Brightest in dungeons, Liberty! thou art') delays the subject, so that the paradox comes first. Liberty's 'habitation' is the heart, a word with biblical overtones of God's dwelling-place (e.g. Psalm 26:8). Liberty is thus imagined as a deity whose temple is the heart, preparing for the sestet's sacred imagery of altar and holy place.

sources.cite: E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet
The Bible (KJV), Psalm 26:8

title: 'The heart which love of thee alone can bind'
short: The only bond that holds the free heart is its love of liberty itself.
body: Byron turns the vocabulary of imprisonment (bind, fetters) against itself: the heart is bound only by love of freedom. The repetition 'the heart-- / The heart' and 'to fetters... To fetters' gives the octave a rhetorical, oratorical quality, like a speech in a liberal cause.

sources.cite: E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet

title: the damp vault's dayless gloom
short: The dungeons of Chillon lie below the level of Lake Geneva, damp and without daylight.
body: Byron's own note describes the castle's range of dungeons beneath the lake level, the pillars with rings for fetters, and a beam on which prisoners were executed. 'Dayless' is a strong compound meaning without daylight. The Prisoner of Chillon itself describes the light that enters through a crevice and the sound of the lake beating against the walls.

sources.cite: E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'dayless, adj.'

title: martyrdom
short: Prisoners for freedom win victory for their country by their suffering, as martyrs bear witness.
body: A martyr (Greek martys, witness) testifies to a faith by suffering or death. Byron transfers the Christian idea to political liberty: the imprisoned patriot's endurance spreads 'Freedom's fame' on every wind. The language anticipates the sestet's religious imagery, where the prison becomes a holy place and its floor an altar. Bonivard did not die at Chillon; he was released in 1536 and lived on until 1570.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'martyr, n.'
E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet

title: Freedom's winged fame
short: The report of their sacrifice flies everywhere; Fame was traditionally a winged goddess.
body: Virgil's Fama (Aeneid IV.173-188) is a swift winged monster who spreads report through cities. Byron's alliteration ('Freedom's fame finds') gives the line the ring of a rallying cry. The octave ends here; the poem turns with the direct address to Chillon. The image fits Byron's own situation in 1816, a celebrity exile whose fame travelled across Europe, though the sonnet keeps the focus on the prisoner's cause.

sources.cite: Virgil, Aeneid IV.173-188
E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet

title: the sonnet's form
short: A Petrarchan-type sonnet: octave on abstract Liberty (abbaacca), sestet on the particular prison (cdcdcd).
body: The octave rhymes Mind/bind/consigned/wind against art/heart and gloom/martyrdom, varying the usual abbaabba; the sestet alternates place/trace/efface with trod/sod/God. The volta at line 9 moves from the general to the particular, from Liberty to Chillon and its prisoner. The sestet runs on by enjambment across 'trod, / Until' and 'a sod, / By Bonnivard!', so that the name falls with emphasis at the start of line 13.

sources.cite: E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet
Jerome J. McGann, ed., Lord Byron: The Complete Poetical Works, vol. 4 (Oxford, 1986), commentary on the Sonnet on Chillon

title: a holy place, an altar
short: The prison is sanctified by suffering: its floor becomes an altar of sacrifice, a place of pilgrimage.
body: God tells Moses at the burning bush, 'the place whereon thou standest is holy ground' (Exodus 3:5). The altar recalls also the martyrs of Revelation 6:9-10, the souls 'under the altar' crying for justice against their oppressors, which anticipates the appeal to God in the final line. Byron's description makes Chillon a shrine of the liberal cause; the castle did become a destination for Romantic tourists, partly because of Byron.

sources.cite: The Bible (KJV), Exodus 3:5
The Bible (KJV), Revelation 6:9-10

title: the worn pavement
short: Bonivard paced his cell so long that his steps wore a track in the stone floor, as though it were turf.
body: Byron's note records that 'in the pavement the steps of Bonnivard have left their traces'. The simile 'as if thy cold pavement were a sod' (turf) compares the trodden stone to a worn footpath in grass.

sources.cite: E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet

title: Bonnivard
short: François Bonivard (1493-1570), Prior of St Victor near Geneva, imprisoned at Chillon from 1530 until 1536 by Charles III, Duke of Savoy.
body: Bonivard supported Genevan independence against the Dukes of Savoy. He was seized in 1530 and confined in Chillon until the castle was taken by the Bernese in March 1536. 'Bonnivard' is Byron's spelling. After his release he became a citizen of Geneva, a chronicler and a member of its councils. Byron's tale invents brothers who die beside him, and the French account Byron printed as an appendix is itself partly unhistorical.

sources.cite: E. H. Coleridge, ed., The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. 4 (1901), introduction to The Prisoner of Chillon, Advertisement and notes to the sonnet
Jerome J. McGann, ed., Lord Byron: The Complete Poetical Works, vol. 4 (Oxford, 1986), commentary on the Sonnet on Chillon

title: 'appeal from tyranny to God'
short: The worn marks are a legal appeal against tyrants to the highest court, God's justice.
body: To appeal is to take a case to a higher court. Byron's prayer that none should efface the marks makes them permanent evidence against the oppressor. The final line joins political and religious language: liberty's martyrs are vindicated not by men but by God, echoing the martyrs under the altar in Revelation who ask how long their blood will go unjudged.
